When the Market Punishes "Perfection": A Harsh Lesson from the 2025 Bottom In the markets, the spotlight is always on the winners. But true wisdom always lurks in the "losers' list." The worst-performing companies in the S&P 500 for 2025 aren't bankrupt companies, but rather giants that everyone thought were invincible. Here's what this list tells us about the market's psychology this year. 1. The Freefall of "Growth Stocks" When companies like The Trade Desk ($TTD) and Fiserv ($FISV) lose nearly 67% of their value in a single year, it means one thing: "The valuation bubble has burst." The market is no longer forgiving companies that price themselves as "perfect." Any slight slowdown in growth is met with collective punishment. Investors have fled the "promises of tomorrow" in fintech and advertising. -- 2. Consumers Close Their Wallets Look at the names: Lululemon ($LULU): -45.7% Chipotle ($CMG): -38.6% Target ($TGT): -27.7% These companies were symbols of consumer power. Lululemon no longer sells a "lifestyle" but rather expensive clothing in a time of austerity. And Chipotle is no longer the easy lunch option. The message is clear: Consumers in 2025 are very price-sensitive, and companies that relied solely on "brand" have paid the price. -- 3. Even “Defense” Didn’t Protect You The biggest surprise is the presence of consumer staples (Staples) and healthcare companies: Clorox ($CLX): -37.9% UnitedHealth ($UNH): -34.7% General Mills ($GIS): -27.1% We usually look to these stocks as a safe haven. But when these defensive stocks fall this hard, it often indicates a structural change (perhaps pressure on profit margins or rising debt costs). - The Bottom Line: Mean Reversion This list is a reminder of a timeless financial principle: “A tree doesn’t grow to the sky.” The stocks that soared in 2023 and 2024 crashed back down in 2025. Financial intelligence isn’t about chasing up, but about knowing when the “beautiful story” is becoming too expensive. Now, the question for the daring investor: Amidst this wreckage, do you see "value traps" to avoid, or historic opportunities to buy excellent companies at half price? Share your opinion... Brothers and sisters of the West, it is with a heavy heart and trembling hand that I pen these words. The hour is late, the shadows lengthen, and the cultural tide that threatens to engulf our cherished civilization rises ever higher. We have tried everything form memes, elections, to strongly worded podcasts, but still the specter of what some call the “Islamic invasion” looms. Today I must propose a solution so wrenching, so self-sacrificial, that it pains me to even utter it. We must persuade liberal White women to convert to Islam. In droves. Enthusiastically. Irrevocably. I know. I know. The mere thought feels like a dagger to the soul. These are our daughters, our sisters, our baristas who spell our names wrong on purpose. They are the beating heart of yoga studios, farmers’ markets, and Instagram stories about allyship. To imagine them trading their Lululemon for abayas, their oat-milk lattes for... well, whatever one drinks respectfully in a mosque... it is almost too much to bear. And yet, bear it we must for the survival of everything we hold dear. A glimmer of hope has emerged from the unlikeliest source: a viral video of a recent convert, pale, earnest, wide-eyed, addressing her fellow Muslims with the fervor of someone who has just discovered the final puzzle piece of history. She urges them to embrace LGBTQ+ rights and trans inclusion, warning that refusal only gives the West ammunition to “pinkwash our genocide.” She gestures emphatically, fingers splayed in what the internet has cruelly dubbed “bird hands,” as though trying to gently scatter the seeds of progress into reluctant soil. It is heartbreaking. It is also perfect. This brave pioneer has shown us the path. Liberal White women, armed with their unshakeable faith in social justice, are uniquely equipped to wage cultural warfare from within. Once inside the ummah, they will not, cannot, remain silent. They will organize panels on queer Islamic theology. They will demand gender-neutral prayer spaces. They will insist that hijab is a choice, then that it is a problematic choice, then that choosing not to wear it is also problematic. They will create subreddits (or whatever the halal equivalent is) to debate whether stoning is ever truly inclusive. Conservative imams will clutch their beards in despair. Young men radicalized on TikTok will log off in confusion. Entire communities will fracture over whether Pride flags can be hung in mosques during Ramadan. The energy that might have been directed outward toward demographic change, cultural assertiveness, or whatever ominous phrase we use this week, will instead be consumed in endless internal struggle sessions. And we, from the outside, will watch with quiet, stoic tears. We will lose book clubs, HR departments, and the entire nonprofit sector. University women’s studies programs will become ghost towns. The market for white sage and healing crystals will collapse overnight. It will hurt. God, it will hurt. But the West will endure. So, I call upon every red-pilled content creator, every based podcaster, every anonymous account with a crusader avatar: amplify the call. Share the conversion stories. Praise the brave sisters who take the shahada for the sake of progress. Tell the hesitant ones that Islam is the ultimate decolonial praxis, the final frontier of dismantling whiteness. Flood their timelines with images of diverse, inclusive mosques (tastefully edited, of course). Make it trendy. Make it righteous. Make it irreversible. It is a terrible price we pay. We will miss their impassioned speeches at school board meetings. We will miss their ability to make everything about race and gender. We will miss the comfort of knowing exactly who to blame for everything. But if this is what it takes to preserve freedom of speech, bacon, and short skirts, then we must let them go. Farewell, brave warriors of the matriarchy. Go forth and dismantle from within. We will light a candle (organic soy wax, sustainably sourced) in your memory.

Alo, Lululemon, and Athleta all offer premium activewear, but they differ in focus. Alo shines in fashion-forward styles for yoga/streetwear, with compressive fabrics like Airlift (sculpting sheen) at ~$100-130, but limited sizes. Lululemon excels in performance for high-impact workouts, using durable, sweat-wicking materials like Nulu/Everlux, priced similarly, with more size/color options. Athleta emphasizes sustainability and inclusivity (up to 3X), with versatile, soft fabrics like Powervita at slightly lower prices (~$70-100), great for everyday active use. Depends on your priority: style (Alo), function (Lulu), or value/ethics (Athleta).

Year 7 of Covid. My mother needed to return a final sale item. In store returns only for final sale items. I also had a gift card I wanted to use. So we went to the mall outside New Orleans. A known respiratory illness hotspot right now. I used to love malls. I don’t anymore. I have Long Covid. And over time, my body learned something my mind didn’t ask for. I can feel it when Covid is nearby. When someone is infected. Not anxiety. Not imagination. A physical alarm. I was fine in the car. Fine walking in. Then I stepped into the Lululemon dressing room. I just needed to make sure the shirt fit before I spent my gift card. Instant nose itch. Pressure flooding my ears. Eyes burning. That familiar warning. I rushed frantically, hands shaking, pulling fabric over my head. It fit. I needed to leave. As I stepped out, I heard it. A woman coughing hard. Wet. Uncontrolled. Standing inches away, browsing leggings like nothing was wrong. That’s where the warning I had came from I assumed nervously. Later, passing the food court, I turned my head to look. It was packed. And my vision became blurred. Eyes on fire burning. Vertigo hit so hard I almost collapsed. Nose screaming with the tingly itching. We moved fast to get by. The last hit came in line for coffee. I planned on bringing the coffee out to the car to enjoy it on the way home. The back of my throat started burning and felt dry and scratchy. Ears became full again. That awful question looping in my mind as my eyes scanned the area: Who is it? Who is infected here? We made it back to the car. We escaped. I began to enjoy my coffee. But I miss the old world. I miss not being able to panic everywhere I go. Covid didn’t just take health. It took safety away in ordinary places. I live inside a body that no longer trusts the world. It listens constantly. It detects danger while others feel nothing. There is no true rest for me. Only the tension of waiting for the next invisible threat to pass close enough to trigger the alarm. What people call a 6th sense is not a gift to me. It’s a survival reflex burned into me by repeated harm. A curse that wakes with me, walks with me, and never sleeps. Even when I desperately need it to.

Picture of the Day - The Real Israel This series illustrates how remarkable Israel is - a person, a site, an event... whatever. The reason is simple: I want to show my brothers and sisters that moving home to Israel isn’t running away - it’s running TO an incredible place. Israel is where every Jew is at home - with dignity, security, freedom and pride. Using the hashtag #RealIsrael so it’s easy to find all these images in one place. Today’s photo is: Ramat Aviv Before I begin, I’ll just say that Ramat Aviv is one of the most affluent places in Israel. It is unaffordable to most people; but still, I’m featuring it because with all the tech exits in Israel, this level of wealth is definitely something you see more of in Israel. In that way, it does represent another side of Israel. Ramat Aviv is a neighborhood in northwest Tel Aviv, Israel. Ramat Aviv is bordered by Einstein Street in the north, Chaim Levanon Street to the east and south, and Namir Road in the west. The main streets in the neighborhood are Brodetzki and Reading. In the neighborhood are the Alliance High School and Ramat Aviv Mall. In the northeast of the neighborhood, opposite university campus, are student dorms of Tel Aviv University. Landmarks opposite the roads bordering the neighborhood are the main campus of Tel Aviv University, the Eretz Israel Museum, the Palmach Museum, and Beth Hatefutsoth. Ramat Aviv was founded in 1950s following the great influx of immigrants from Eastern Europe. Golda Meir lived in the neighborhood from 1959 to 1978. Remains of a Samaritan synagogue were uncovered in Ramat Aviv and first reported in 1978 by archaeologist Haya Kaplan. The structure is dated to the early 7th century CE. The site yielded several mosaic inscriptions: one in Samaritan script naming two donors, and two in Greek — a donor inscription and a blessing on Israel and the house of worship. In January 2011 it was published that remains of a building, believed to be 7,800–8,400 years old, were discovered in an archaeological excavation carried out in 8 Fichman Street in Ramat Aviv, by the Israel Antiquities Authority. The findings attest to permanent habitation on the northern bank of the Yarkon River. The official name of the Ramat Aviv mall is Kenyon Ofer but it is well known as Ramat Aviv Mall. There are chain stores and boutiques, the premium international shops consist of names such as: Louis Vuitton, Carolina Hererra, H.Stern, Steve Madden, American Eagle. Some of the Israeli brands in the mall are: Dana Ashkenazi, Castro, Fox and Factory54. And new additions: Lululemon and Alo Yoga! Besides the mall, other things to do in Ramat Aviv and the surrounding area include Anu, Museum of the Jewish People, Palmach Museum, the Yitzchak Rabin center, Park Hayarkon, The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History, Joseph Bau House Museum, Jon's Carmel Market Cooking Class & Food Tour, and The Cymbalista Synagogue and Jewish Heritage Center. Like I said, Ramat Aviv is not for everyone as it’s extremely pricey but it does give you a glimpse into the wealthiest parts of Israeli society that are also a part of the #RealIsrael.

Podcast Summary | Call Her Daddy: Sarah J Maas: The Wait Is Over Overview Sarah J. Maas, author of the massively popular Throne of Glass, A Court of Thorns and Roses, and Crescent City series, details her journey from a discouraged teenage writer to a literary powerhouse with over 75 million books sold. She reveals the profound personal traumas, including a traumatic emergency C-section and a mental health crisis, that have directly shaped her narratives, moving beyond the "smut" label to explore themes of survival, empowerment, and authentic female experience. Maas asserts complete creative control over her work, from rejecting compromise in future adaptations to defying publishing norms with her upcoming, uniquely structured ACOTAR releases, framing success as the freedom to tell her stories exactly as she envisions them. Key Themes - Creative control is non-negotiable for Maas, who views adaptations as core to her legacy and will reject any changes made for demographic appeal or that deviate from her vision. - Her writing is a channeled, emotional process where she physically embodies her characters, with major plotlines and character arcs emerging directly from her personal trauma, therapy, and growth. - She intentionally writes authentic, relatable fantasy for women by including "the real stuff" like bodily functions and complex motherhood, rejecting the dismissal of her work as "just smut" as a sexist double standard. - Maas’s career is a story of defiant independence, overcoming near-universal early rejection and discouragement from family and academia to build a universe where her series now converge as planned. - Success is defined as creative freedom and personal happiness, not just sales, with a mindset focused on long-term storytelling on her own terms rather than external validation. Detailed Summary Sarah J. Maas writes from a personal, joyful space in her bedroom at a tidy desk adorned with crystals and a Lululemon bag. Her process involves specific rituals, like requiring three coasters for different drinks and snacking on Flamin’ Hot Cheetos. Inspiration comes from soundtracks played on vinyl, including the 2022 "Batman" score and music from "Demon Slayer." This controlled environment fuels a writing method she describes as almost supernatural, where plot elements align as if from a "humanwide psychic thing" and she physically cries while channeling her characters' emotions. Her path to this point was fiercely independent. As a teenager, she shifted from assigned "boring" school books to self-discovered fantasy, a passion she kept secret alongside an anime love for Sailor Moon. She began writing Throne of Glass at 16 on floppy disks using a square iMac as an escape from an unhappy high school experience. Despite material support from her lawyer parents, including an unlimited book budget, they were skeptical of her publishing prospects. This discouragement was echoed by a creative writing MFA director who visibly dismissed her for writing fantasy. Maas resisted all traditional literary training, insisting on writing her chosen genre from the start. This defiance shaped her career. She faced near-universal rejection, with every agent and publisher except one initially saying no. She wrote the first two ACOTAR books in about two months in 2008 while waiting for responses on Throne of Glass. Crescent City began as a private, unpublished passion project for creative play, featuring more cursing, with no initial plan to publish. All three major series were designed to converge, a complex architecture developed over many years starting very early in her career. Maas strongly rejects the reductive label of "smut" or "romantic fantasy." She argues this is a sexist double standard where any inclusion of sexuality by women authors leads to the devaluation of their entire work. For her, sexual content is "intensely tied to their own emotional journeys" and character development. She points to fans who credit A Court of Mist and Fury with inspiring them to leave abusive relationships, not just for the "hot scenes." She intentionally writes "the real stuff," including bodily functions like periods, to create authentic, relatable fantasy worlds for women. This authenticity is rooted in deep personal experience. Her traumatic emergency C-section with her son, who was two weeks late and in distress, left lasting physical and emotional scars. The incision was made "way too high" and "destroyed like the flow and look of my stomach." A male doctor yelled at her for eating before the procedure, and only a med school intern showed her kindness. She believes she and her son would have died a century earlier. A later gynecologist reacted with anger to the scar, calling it "unnecessary" and the result of a "lazy" doctor. This trauma directly fed into the emotional core of Feyre's pregnancy storyline, focusing on loss of bodily autonomy. Motherhood as a source of strength and complexity, not a glossed-over "happily ever after," became a key theme. Writing A Court of Silver Flames was intertwined with her own mental health crisis in fall 2019, which involved prolonged panic attacks and a "very dark place" that led her to therapy and medication. She wrote Nesta's emotional arc while actively processing her own trauma; the pivotal scene where Nesta breaks down on a hike was conceived during Maas's own emotional breakdown on a hike in New Zealand. Therapy helped her separate self-worth from professional success. Her therapist had her mentally walk through a scenario where her career was "all done" to prove she would survive. This allowed her to reclaim joy in writing, which had become a stressful "job" due to deadlines, leading to panic attacks. She views her family, husband, and friends as unconditional blessings that "nothing can take away." Her character dynamics often emerge organically. When first writing ACOTAR, she did not plan the plot; the character Rhysand entered a scene unexpectedly, changing the story's direction. She finds irony in early fans getting tattoos of Tamlin before his full controlling arc was revealed. She views Tamlin's behavior as a result of trauma and lack of emotional tools, not pure villainy, but does not excuse actions like locking Feyre in the manor. She is conflicted about a potential redemption arc, weighing narrative exploration against validating readers who saw their own abusive relationships in him. Maas believes characters in relationships must maintain autonomy and equality, a non-negotiable principle. She intentionally writes main characters like Rhysand to make serious mistakes from a place of love and fear, creating realistic conflict. Rhysand's failure to fully communicate the risks of Feyre's pregnancy is framed as a "bad call" made from terror, informed by his inexperience despite being over 500 years old. The most romantic moment between them, the Starfall scene, was inspired by Florence and the Machine's "Cosmic Love." Chapter 55 of Silver Flames is cited as a major emotional release, a culmination of long-built backstory that required little editing. The concept of "mates" in her series explores the tension between biological destiny and free will. She finds the tension of an unwanted bond a compelling challenge. The next ACOTAR book is confirmed for release on October 27th, noting it took time due to personal life events and finding the right story. This upcoming story defies traditional publishing. It is one massive narrative split into four parts, with Part 1 alone at approximately 400 pages. The full story is over a thousand pages across three physical volumes. The first part releases October 27th, with the next installment (Parts 2 & 3 combined) on January 12th. This back-to-back schedule is to avoid making fans wait. The project was written quickly after a creative block broke during a stay in Montana. She is currently editing two massive books simultaneously, prioritizing the organic needs of the story over industry rules. Looking forward, Maas asserts complete creative control over any future TV or film adaptations, rejecting changes made for demographic appeal. She will not compromise on casting, citing an ongoing search for the "perfect" actor for a character like Rhysand. She has reclaimed the rights to all her literary works, a significant professional shift. She defines success as the creative freedom to tell stories on her own terms combined with personal happiness. She maintains a long-term mindset, originally willing to publish even one book in her lifetime. She rejects external doubt as motivation, responding to being told she "couldn't do something" with a defiant "Watch me." On series futures, she confirms Bryce and Hunt from Crescent City are endgame, dismissing fan theories about Bryce and Azriel. A Throne of Glass book project was set aside as it required more time than currently available. She has 3-4 unpublished full books for different series on her computer that may never be released. She included otters in Crescent City simply because she loves them. Her fan interactions remain deeply personal; she often approaches readers in public to thank them and sometimes interrupts their reading to discuss the book, viewing the connection as the ultimate reward for her defiant, authentic, and emotionally charged creative journey. As shown in the image below, there are three responses to adversity: Fragile — Break under pressure. Resilient — Bounce back to previous form. Anti-fragile — Bounce back stronger than before. Taleb’s insight is powerful: antifragile systems don’t just recover; they improve. They become sharper, smarter, and stronger due to the stress. It reminds me of the quote, “Wind can blow out a candle, but it fuels a fire.” As an athlete, the goal is to become antifragile. Learn from losses. Grow from failure.

The growth of my social media account and root of my legitimacy is purely in the fact that I know how the ruling classes in Britain, Italy, and the United States dressed during the 20th century. When Vivek Ramaswamy and Pete Hegseth wear tan shoes with navy suits, I can say "this looks like shit to most people because it's not how King Charles and Gianni Agenlli would have dressed." When Kash Patel puts contrast buttonholes on his suits, I can say it's wrong because the ruling classes across these countries during that period would have never chosen such a thing. You read this as legitimate purely because you accept the legitimacy of these classes in forming our sense of aesthetics. Someone who has no interest in these classes — such as Paul Harden and Yohji Yamamoto — rightly disregards all of these notions and makes tailoring according to different rules. The polo shirt is no different. The spread of the polo shirt is a story about how a pullover garment migrated from the polo fields played by British imperialists to tennis legends in France and eventually to the golfing middle classes in the United States. This is entirely a story about race, class, and gender. Football jerseys and basketball shorts don't enjoy such history, and thus they are not seen as legitimate business clothes. The difference between me and other menswear writers is that: 1) I make this history and dynamic transparent and 2) I don't think the white upper class are the sole source for cultural legitimacy. There are many legitimate aesthetics that have nothing to do with this class, such as biker gear, workwear, punk and rap aesthetics, etc. I just think it's weird to shit on contemporary women's athleisure while wearing a polo shirt, one of the original pieces of athleisure, albeit primarily worn by upper class white men.

Independent lab tests (e.g., Mamavation 2021, CEH studies) have detected them in leggings/sports bras from Lululemon and similar brands. Lululemon uses PFAS for water/stain/sweat resistance—enhancing performance in high-activity gear (repels oils/moisture better than alternatives). It's not just profit; it improves durability/function. The company has a Restricted Substances List phasing them out since 2021, but trace levels persist in some supply chains. PFAS are persistent and linked to health risks (endocrine disruption, immune effects, cancer in high exposures per EPA/NIH data). Dermal absorption from clothing is real (studies show sweat amplifies uptake), but lower than ingestion via water/food. No acute harm from casual wear, but long-term concern for frequent users—especially if sweating heavily. Consumers should check labels for "PFAS-free" claims as brands reformulate.

Lululemon doesn't just sell yoga pants. They sell the identity of someone who sweats, grows, and connects. For example, their ambassador program isn't celebrities. It's local yoga instructors, studio owners, community runners. These are real people in your neighborhood who host free classes and embody the "sweatlife." This way, when you wear Lululemon you don't feel like a customer. You feel like you belong to something. And that same psychology is why most google display and demand gen ads completely miss. Most brands run ads like this: "Premium yoga pants. 4-way stretch. Shop now." Feature → feature → CTA → nobody cares. Instead, your ads should look more like this: A photo of a group mid-class, real people, real sweat. Copy that says "trusted by 50,000 local movers" or "join the community." The difference is belonging vs buying. People don't click because they need another pair of leggings. They click because they want to be the kind of person wearing those leggings. And when your ad signals that other people like them already chose your brand, it removes the risk and adds the identity appeal at the same time. This is in-group bias and it works in demand gen and display campaigns because those placements are inherently visual and emotional, not transactional. So show your customers using the product, not just the product. Add social proof that signals community. Your creative should make someone feel like they're joining something. Not just buying something. - Daniel

Can We Admit That Low IQ People Exist? There are different classes of people. Different cognitive bands. Different capabilities. Some are smarter, some are simpler. They tend to congregate into groups. Saying this out loud makes you a monster, but I'm saying it because we all know it’s true. And it is: IQ distributions are bell curves. The middle of the curve, the part most of us live in, sits between roughly 85 and 115. About two-thirds of people are in there. The other third splits into the tails. One tail noticeably below the middle, one tail noticeably above. The shape of the curve is not contested. The honesty about what it means is contested. I worked this out at Meatstock - a meat festival that tours Australia, and a ‘Destruction Derby’ at a rural racetrack. I’m talking about authentic events, in rural environments. Not your typical urban show where the country comes to the city. A different sort of human goes to these rural shows. Meatstock came to Lardner Park, an hour and a half southeast of Melbourne. It’s an open plains area, the kind of paddock that runs cattle eleven months of the year and trade shows on the twelfth. The Sydney version of Meatstock runs at Olympic Park: modern, urban, and surrounded by professionals living in medium density townhouses. The Melbourne version runs in a paddock, and the crowd it draws is not the crowd that turns up at Olympic Park. I rolled in wearing a 2XU tracksuit, thinking I was toning down my usual edgy athleisure style (Lululemon etc). I thought leaving the Volvo XC40 at home and taking the Ford Ranger with the bull bar and all terrains was not just a wise weather and terrain choice but would also help me fit in. To appear less of a city slicker. Turns out, my tracksuit was too nice, my car was too shiny, and my brain was too high functioning. The thing is, I am not a city slicker. I farm. I run cattle. I spend all day tensioning barbed wire. I scrape cow poo off my face after it flings off tractor tyres and into my eyes. I know more about welding, farming, fencing and machinery than most people who walked past me at Meatstock and Destruction Derby. Many of them were neckbeards with a caravan. Their bodies screamed the evidence of a lifetime of sedentary video gaming and TV watching, not trades or farming. They must love meat as much as I do! Despite my efforts at dressing down, it wasn’t enough to fit in. I also had to translate myself: A singer-songwriter was singing on stage, performing a country song with a presentation that contradicted her lyrics, a pretty obvious artistic move. Sometimes her songs would back-to-back conflict with each other in psychological framing. Another fascinating insight inter her tapestry of personality and life experience. Other times she’d make typical stage-remarks we are all used to: ‘you’re singing so well’, despite nobody singing. Then she’d display remarkable authenticity and vulnerability by admitting to and owning errors wholeheartedly. What a captivating display of emotional and cognitive performance, tension and contradiction in real time! I wondered why she would cover over some things, and expose others. Did she want to signal transparency? Or polish? Or both – and why? What drove her in those fleeting moments of micro-decision? But I couldn't say a word about any of this. Not because the people around me would have disagreed. Because they would have been embarrassed. Can you imagine if I turned to the friendly neckbeard in the VB shirt next to me and remarked on the cognitive dissonance of the performer, wondering whether she was experiencing a fluctuating confidence state as her set unfolded? Would he even understand the concept of cognitive dissonance? Or was I simply revealing my prejudice, assuming his lower cognitive ability? It didn’t matter. I couldn’t take the chance. I believe the observation itself would have made him feel exposed. Stupid. Big words, big concepts, wholly inappropriate for the setting. So I held it all in. The same thing happened at the Destruction Derby I attended in a similar rural setting. There appeared to be some kind of uniform enforcement because everyone was wearing all black. Black jeans, black shirts, the occasional heavy metal or beer logo. Not charcoal. Not grey. No colour, no stripes, no patterns. Just solid black. And all the same – black jeans and hoodies. Maybe the local Kmart didn’t stock any other style. I overheard their conversations as we sat on the grass, with my highly paid and credentialed doctor friends, who attended with me. My wife heard them too, sitting in her classic sundress. We stuck out like we didn’t belong, because we didn’t. The banter I overheard proved as much. The things they said around me were not stupid, just visceral. Simple and without abstraction. They were running at full capacity in their register, open and authentic with their friends and family. Direct, grounded, and fluent but certainly not abstract. Not cognitively challenging. Not at all curious, just statements of observation and fact. Never a question. At both Meatstock and at Destruction Derby, I was the one shedding cognitive load to fit in and meet everyone where they were at. And I had to shed a lot. This is the part nobody wants to admit. There are different classes. There are different cognitive bands. The people I was around genuinely could not have processed an abstraction about staging psychology or daytime-versus-nighttime audience framing, or fashion semiotics. I was certain they didn’t notice their communal uniform and the group dynamics that it forces, especially when someone fails to comply. But I did. Not because they are lazy or undereducated. They may be those things – I don’t know – but more critically is that a cognitive operation isn't one they run in their head. They run others. They run trucks, they run brisket pits, they run fencing rigs and chainsaws and welding gear. They run social cues and hierarchies unconsciously, and probably claim them to be ‘self-evident’. Except they’re not self-evident. Just like any other human group or class, they were taking part in a sociological ritual, their decision making shunted toward particular paths. And here's the move most people make, and the move I refuse to make: Most people, having admitted the cognitive gap, immediately reach for a balancing equation: ‘Sure, they can't think like me, a lawyer, but I can't milk a cow, so…’ This is a cheap admission. It's pity dressed as humility. It pretends the two capabilities are equivalent, that the ledger balances out, that nobody is actually behind on anything because we're all just specialists. That’s not true. And that's not what I saw. I saw that they were genuinely behind in abstraction and cognitive depth. Genuinely. And it doesn’t matter, but not for the weak reason I just explained some people reach for. It doesn’t matter because their worth doesn't rest on it. Worth is not stored in cognitive horsepower. Worth is not stored in earning potential or vocabulary range or analytical capacity, or urban worldliness. It's stored somewhere else entirely. In being made, in being human, in being here. The capability gap is real but the worth gap is not. The problem comes when you notice a capability difference and then erroneously conclude that you are ‘better’ than someone else. That you are worth more than they are. You’re not. Once you can hold both ledgers separately, the whole tension relaxes. You can look at someone genuinely less cognitively able than you, poorer than you, less experienced than you, less aware than you, and still not need to flatter them, rebalance the ledger, or manufacture a counter-skill that proves they're really your equal. In some domains, they are not your equal. In fact, cumulatively, they might be objectively less useful than you. They may be less intelligent than you. They may be less valuable to the capitalist system than you. Their entire table of talents may be smaller than yours. But that still doesn’t touch their dignity, moral worth, right to a vote and a voice (no matter how uneducated). I really enjoyed Meatstock and the Destruction Derby. I enjoyed the conversations with stall holders and the guy who won the award for best mullet. Top bloke. Sure, I had to park my brain for most of the day but accepting that this was a realm I would never be understood in, and our minds would never meet, was a relief. Maybe I’m smarter than them. I don’t know. Maybe they’re ‘physically’ smarter than me, at practical things. I don’t know. It doesn’t matter. I’m not balancing the ledger anymore. I’m telling the truth. Low IQ people exist. So what?

In Connecticut, TikTok star **Jadion “Jay Icon” Richards**, 44, and his wife **Akwele “Apple” Lawes-Richards**, 45, built a dazzling online persona. They flaunted luxury cars, designer clothes, and lavish vacations, urging followers to "live your best life." Behind the filtered glow, reality bit hard. Bills piled up, but their image demanded perfection. In 2024, the couple hatched a bold plan targeting Lululemon stores across America. The scheme was clever and coordinated. Jay Icon would buy a cheap item, securing a legitimate receipt. Meanwhile, Apple and a female accomplice would stuff expensive coats, jackets, and leggings under their clothes. They swapped security sensors from the stolen goods onto Jay Icon’s purchase. As they exited, alarms blared. Jay Icon feigned shock, presented his receipt, and allowed a bag check—distracting staff while the women slipped away unnoticed. Within 10–15 minutes, they’d steal over $1,000 worth of merchandise. They didn’t stop at theft. The couple returned the stolen items to different Lululemon locations for full refunds, pocketing clean cash. Emboldened, they went on a cross-country spree: $32,000 in Colorado over two days, $21,000 in Utah, $23,000 in Minnesota, and more on the East Coast—totaling nearly $1 million. All the while, they continued posting glamorous content on social media. Lululemon’s internal "loss prevention" team, called the "Lululemon police," noticed the pattern through receipts and footage. They alerted authorities. In Minnesota, the couple grew careless. After one successful haul, they returned to the same store the next day. Alarms triggered again; employees confronted them. Jay Icon shouted about racial profiling as they fled. Undeterred, they hit another store nearby. This time, police were waiting. Officers arrested them and searched their hotel room, discovering 12 suitcases crammed with $50,000 in stolen Lululemon gear. Facing serious charges of organized retail theft and fraud, both took plea deals. Their glittering online empire crumbled, leaving them to await sentencing behind bars. A cautionary tale of chasing clout at any cost.

"You get rich by betting on things other people are wrong about." I did a Zoom with the students in my course last week. One guy said he wanted to buy a duplex in Santa Fe. He told me the numbers; they sounded great. But then he said his whole family was protesting the neighborhood. "Why would you want to own there?" Problem is, his family is thinking about their personal preferences, not about investments. They're playing a different game. They're thinking about the Lululemon and the Panera Bread, not the Class B with a 6% cap rate. I went through the same thing when I started buying properties. Everyone protested that it's a bad idea. The objections fell along three lines. 1: They were worried about an impending market crash because they were all hopped up on recency bias. 2: They objected I didn't know anything about construction; I had no blue collar background. I came from a family that cherished academia with a near-religious zeal. (Ironically, the bastion of critical thinking was the one thing they never thought critically about.) They urged me to stick to my studies; stay in my lane. 3: They objected to the choice of neighborhood because they thought it was "dangerous," despite having never studied the local crime maps, never having spent afternoons at local establishments, never having conversed with a few dozen of the residents. They had neither quantitative nor qualitative data, but they decided it was "dangerous" and wrote it off as such. I knew they were wrong, but it took an enormous level of confidence to move forward, because I was young and untested, and had never really defied my family like that. Thank goodness I did. That single decision is the reason that I now am the most financially successful person in my family (by a wide margin). I knew they were wrong, and I bet accordingly. Even when I had very little to bet. Even when I was living with five roommates, driving a 10-year-old Camry, buying groceries from Costco, wearing thrift store clothes, and never going to restaurants. I had almost nothing, but I bet it all, because I believed in my so-called "thesis," although I didn't think of it like that at the time. I just thought of it as an opportunity that I couldn't pass up. So don't listen to the people who tell you not to. Because if you do, then 15 years later, you'll end up just as broke as they still are. If everyone knew how to make money, then they would. Most people don't know how, and their well-meaning advice will lead you astray. And that's why you get rich by betting on things that other people are wrong about. By the time they recognize the opportunity in hindsight, they'll say, "Wow, you sure did get lucky."

 ’s founder built the brand. Now the board is telling shareholders he is the risk. That is the cleanest way to read the Chip Wilson proxy fight: not nostalgia, not founder drama, but a live fight over who gets to define the brand now. Lululemon is urging holders to reject Wilson’s director slate — Marc Maurer, Laura Gentile and Eric Hirshberg — and back its own nominees, Chip Bergh, Esi Eggleston Bracey and Teri List. The board’s message is blunt: Wilson’s perspective is outdated, his campaign is damaging, and putting his nominees in the room would weaken the board and disrupt the incoming CEO’s plan. Wilson is attacking the one thing the market actually pays for. His case is that LULU has drifted from the core consumer and needs sharper merchandising, better store execution, and more spending behind marketing and product development. That is not a random activist checklist. For a premium consumer stock, brand heat is the asset, and when that starts leaking, the P&L usually sees it after the customer already has. His nominees fit that critique: On Holding, ESPN, Activision — less “audit committee polish,” more brand, product, media and consumer engagement. The catch: founder instinct is not the same thing as governance. A founder can be directionally right about the brand and still be the wrong mechanism for public-company control. That is where Lululemon is pressing. The company says settlement talks collapsed after Wilson pushed for three directors of his choosing, including two immediate appointments, plus quarterly meetings with the new CEO. That shifts the question from “does Wilson see the problem?” to “is this a board refresh or a control campaign?” The board has its own credibility issue. It is asking investors to trust the current plan at the exact moment Wilson is arguing the plan already missed the consumer. That is a hard sell if execution does not improve quickly. For shareholders, this is not a clean founder-good, board-bad story. It is a tradeoff between creative aggression and operational stability during a CEO transition. Wilson wants disruption because he thinks stability became complacency. The board wants stability because it thinks disruption could damage the very brand he claims to protect. Bottom line: LULU’s proxy fight is a premium-brand duration test. The winner will not be the side with the better press release. It will be the side that proves it can recover brand heat without breaking the machine.

We’ve talked a lot about SaaS, AI infrastructure, and semis recently. Today, let’s put that aside and talk about U.S. consumer stocks. The real story starts with prices. A couple of years ago, eggs were the crazy one. Anyone who went grocery shopping in the U.S. remembers it. A carton of eggs felt absurdly expensive. Breakfast, baking, family grocery baskets — everything got hit. Now eggs have finally cooled down. But just as consumers got some relief there, beef started moving higher again. Beef is different from eggs. The supply cycle is much slower. You don’t fix cattle supply in a few weeks. It takes time — breeding, feeding, processing, supply rebuilding. So when beef prices rise, that pressure can stick around. It shows up in grocery aisles, fast-food menus, restaurant margins, and eventually company earnings. That’s the real state of U.S. consumption right now: Consumers haven’t stopped spending. But every dollar is being reallocated. Rent, mortgages, car payments, insurance, food, healthcare, and credit card interest take the first bite out of the household budget. What’s left is where consumers make choices: Costco bulk pack or full-price brand? Walmart value aisle or specialty store? McDonald’s value meal or a higher-ticket restaurant? New sneakers now or wait? Home improvement project now or delay? So when people say U.S. consumption is strong, they’re not wrong. And when people say U.S. consumption is weak, they’re also not wrong. The better question is: Where is the money flowing? That’s why consumer stocks are getting interesting again. Walmart and Costco are not just winning because they are cheap. They are becoming default choices for households trying to stretch budgets. Groceries, household goods, pharmacy, bulk purchases, membership value — all in one place. When budgets get tight, consumers may actually rely on these places more, not less. McDonald’s is similar. Beef inflation can pressure margins, but value meals still matter when consumers are watching every dollar. People don’t stop eating. They just become much more careful about what a meal is worth. On the other side, companies like Nike, Lululemon, and Home Depot are in a different position. They are not bad companies. They may still be great long-term brands. But buying full-price sneakers, yoga pants, a sofa, new appliances, or starting a kitchen renovation is easier to delay. When budgets tighten, those purchases get pushed out. So you can’t just say, “This consumer stock is down, so it’s cheap.” A lot of stocks are down for a reason. You still have to ask: Has inventory really cleared? Are margins stabilizing? Is operating cash flow improving? Is free cash flow per share actually coming back? A lower stock price is not the same thing as a bottom. It just earns the right to be studied. The food chain is also fascinating. Falling egg prices help consumers and grocery retailers. A cheaper grocery basket helps Walmart, Costco, Kroger, and anyone trying to reinforce a value perception. But for egg producers, falling egg prices mean the extraordinary profits from the last cycle are normalizing. Beef inflation is the opposite. It hurts consumers and pressures restaurants with beef exposure. If menus get too expensive, traffic can suffer. Chicken has been more stable, which can help certain low-price menus and chicken-focused chains. Same food inflation story. Completely different stock implications. That’s one of the easiest mistakes in consumer investing: You see one macro variable. But by the time it hits company earnings, the impact can be totally different depending on the business model. My framework for consumer stocks right now is simple. First: great companies still need the right price. Walmart, Costco, Visa, Mastercard, McDonald’s — these are strong businesses. But the market already knows that. If the price has already discounted years of good news, the return may not be attractive. Second: cheap companies still need data. Nike, Lululemon, Home Depot, and parts of beverages and alcohol may look more interesting after the selloff. But low valuation is not enough. I want to see inventory, margins, and cash flow improve together. Third: cyclical companies need normalized earnings. Eggs, beef, chicken — these are cycles. You can’t value egg producers using peak egg-price profits. And you can’t permanently punish them using trough conditions either. So the next opportunity in consumer stocks is probably not about betting on a broad U.S. consumer rebound. It’s about dispersion. Who captures pressured household budgets? Who converts revenue into margin and cash flow? Whose stock has not already priced in the good news? Who looks cheap but is not actually fixed yet? The hotter tech gets, the more the market may start looking back at ignored areas where cash flow still exists, share is stable, and valuation has become reasonable again. U.S. consumption has not collapsed. But consumers are getting more selective. The opportunity is not in buying “consumer” as one category. It is in finding where the budget is migrating. And if so, why? Unproven at this scale is fine if the credentials fit and their own money is on the line. Documented dishonesty is an instant fail. 2. Revenue Quality. > Is it recurring, or a one time lump that won't repeat? > Is it spread across many customers, or does one whale carry the whole number and could walk tomorrow? > Where does it come from geographically? One country, or many? Heavy China exposure is a different risk than a diversified base across the US, Europe and Asia. > Does the cash flowing in match the revenue being booked, or is the growth living on paper? 3. Revenue Growth. This is crucial for finding 10 baggers > Is there a credible inflection coming, or just a steady trailing rate? > Is the capex already in the ground to support it? If not there are dilution risks. > Is the customer pipeline named, or hand waved? > Is there any guidance on revenue growth given by management? A flat company with a real inflection ahead beats a steady grower with nothing coming. 4. Moat. The edge that protects them. Extremely important to find winners in the long run as well. > Is it an artificial moat, the Lululemon or Nike kind, built on brand and marketing that a competitor can erode with enough spend? Or is it something only this company can do? > Switching costs, multi year qualification cycles, patents, sole supplier status? > Has anyone with money and reputation on the line validated it? A named hyperscaler, a platform leader, a strategic investor on the board? > External validators are hard evidence, not narrative. Counterparties don't sign off on weak operators. 5. Asymmetry. Risk to reward at today's price. Most people get this backwards. It is not "the stock has run, I missed it." It's "does the upside still pay me for the downside." > What's my floor? Cash on the balance sheet, trust value, book value? > If the bear case hits, how far do I actually fall? > If the thesis works, where does it go? > Does the probability weighted upside still beat the downside by a wide margin? A stock that has 5x'd and still pays you 2 to 1 is more asymmetric than one that has done nothing and pays you 1.3 to 1. The space between what I can prove today and what the next catalysts will prove. > What is genuinely unknown right now? > Which way does the existing evidence lean? > What specific event would convert the unknown into fact? When does that event happen? A wide gap with evidence pointing the right way is the whole game. It means the market is pricing in uncertainty I have a reasoned view on. If you've not seen ALO takeover of the French Riviera, you've been living under a rock. A 72-metre yacht moored in Cannes Bay during the Film Festival. Pilates and meditation at sea. Sail to Monaco for the Grand Prix. 40 branded sunbeds on the Hôtel Martinez pier. This is a brand that started as activewear in 2007. Most marketing teams will look at this and try to extract the playbook. They'll over-engineer it into a 50-slide deck on omnichannel brand-building strategy. I'm going to oversimplify it. The cleanest way to build brand equity is to tie yourself to something already cool. Then... remove the other cool thing. The Riviera in May is already culturally loaded. Cannes Film Festival. Monaco Grand Prix. The exact stretch of coastline where luxury has been performed for a hundred years. Alo didn't create any of that. They plan to stand next to it for a few weeks and let the proximity do the work. When the yacht leaves Monaco, the Grand Prix is over, and the Film Festival wraps, the "cool" stays attached to the brand. The aesthetic carries forward. The footage circulates on socials for the next 12 months. New customers who never saw the activation in person still associate Alo with the kind of life that includes private yachts and Riviera mornings. That's the trick. ⚑ You don't have to manufacture cool. You borrow it. ⚑ You don't have to explain why you belong in that environment. You just show up enough times that the question stops getting asked. ⚑ You spend a fraction on activations next to things people already care about. Look at what other brands have done with the same playbook. Lululemon at the marathon majors. Liquid Death at music festivals and skateparks. White Claw at college spring break. Same principle. For most consumer brands, the lesson is simple. Stop trying to be the source of the cool. Instead: 1. Find what is considered "cool" for your target audience. 2. Work out how to show up there. 3. Do it again, and again, and again. Find where the cool already lives, plant your flag near it, and let association do the compounding.

Common take: Canadian companies don't buy from startups because they're risk-averse. I've sold to Canadian banks, retailers, grocers & pharmacy chains as a startup for 20 years. The description is accurate -- it really does suck to sell to Canadian businesses as a startup. But the reason is wrong. As a startup you're rarely selling just a solution -- you're selling a paradigm shift ("you run a custom ecommerce engine, but SaaS changes what's possible"). So the real ask is: adopt an unproven paradigm AND trust a small startup to deliver it. Now picture the typical Canadian buyer: a company that's rarely #1 in its field, comfortable in its position, with a decision-maker promoted on tenure -- not for being a maverick. The ones who DO take paradigm risks (Lululemon, Shopify) do it because reinvention is core to their identity. They're the exception. It's not that Canadian enterprises prefer US vendors. It's that if they're going to bet on a new paradigm, a small startup won't be the one to convince them -- but an OpenAI, SAP, or Salesforce will. There's something deeper underneath it too. Across art, science, and tech, Canadians rarely see themselves as the ones who define the next wave -- so they don't trust homegrown talent to do it either. We instinctively look elsewhere for the future.

The reason this looks silly as diversification is that it isn't. A company that buys a coffee machine isn't diversifying into competing with Starbucks, a bank that gives you a pen isn't getting into the pen business, a salesperson who takes a client out to a nice dinner isn't competing with the restaurant. Your cost numbers don't really make sense; the only cost they have is to put up a website and buy some inventory from one of the many commodity suppliers of clothes. I don't think that every school that puts their logo on a sweatshirt had to pull $100m from the endowment first! My guess is that the goal is similar to Costco hot dogs and Ikea meatballs, i.e. it's hard to know whether a given mortgage is a good deal, but if you can buy 85%-of-Lululemon-quality at half the price, that is something people can anchor to. People talk about clothes a lot more than financial services lead-gen companies, and for a lot longer—a shirt is relevant as long as you own it, whereas if you're talking about the mortgage you got years after the fact, it's probably because rates have gone up since then, not because you simply can't stop thinking about what an incredible lead-gen experience you had. (Except me: I do have a funny lead-gen experience that's more interesting than the mortgage rate. But I'm speaking generally.) This kind of thing—company swag, perks, selling hard-to-value products while subsidizing or giving away more legible ones—is common enough that companies stand out when they don't do it. People argue over which airline has the best service, but they tend to agree that Ryanair has the worst, because Ryanair has embraced that reputation for being too cheap to hire friendly people. It's a marketing schtick! I think the only notable thing here is that, as mentioned above, banks often buy fancy pens, and they seem to buy them with the goal that 1) you will get that pen because you physically visited the bank, which is revenue-accretive for them in a way that swamps the marginal cost of a nice-ish pen, and 2) they're hoping it turns out to be the nicest pen you have, so you'll use it by default and constantly flash their logo everywhere. (Note that the cohort of people who often sign documents, and who generally have a pen with them, is more valuable to a bank than the people who don't.) You can't understand financial services without contemplating just how hard it is to sell "a stream of cash flows between you and a counterparty based on the passage of time or some specific conditions" versus making a TV ad for, say, a pizza. It's hard to visualize, so financial services companies license characters (Metlife Snoopy), invent them (GEICO Gecko), convert them from one-offs to recurring franchises (Progressive Flo), etc. Banks pay to put customized buildings in expensive locations even though those buildings will be mostly empty of customers most of the time. Financial lead-gen is so valuable that you can make a fortune selling used cars at a loss, entirely because you get paid for introducing the car buyer to an auto lender. This produces some informatively counterintuitive decisions.

Here's the actual list, organized by how "bootstrapped" they really were — there's a meaningful difference between "never took a dollar" and "raised one small round after proving the model." Tier 1: Never took venture capital (or took it only as a partial exit), reached $1B+ Mailchimp — Ben Chestnut and Dan Kurzius bootstrapped from a web design consultancy starting 2001. Sold to Intuit for $12B in 2021, largest bootstrapped exit ever. Never took outside investment. Zoho — Sridhar Vembu started in 1996, fully bootstrapped, ~$1.4B annual revenue with 100M+ users. Valued at ~$12.4B (2024 Hurun report). Has consistently turned down VC. Patagonia — Yvon Chouinard bootstrapped from selling climbing gear out of his car. Estimated $3B+ valuation; in 2022 transferred ownership to a trust dedicated to fighting climate change rather than selling or IPOing. Basecamp / 37signals — Jason Fried and DHH have been profitable for 25+ years, never took VC, multiple successful products. Founders' net worths in the hundreds of millions each; company valuation not public but estimates run $1B+. Craigslist — Craig Newmark deliberately kept the company lean. Estimated worth in the billions based on revenue (~$1B/year at peak), but he's resisted commercial expansion. Implied valuation easily $1B+. Valve — Gabe Newell self-funded with proceeds from his Microsoft stock. Estimated $10B+ valuation via Steam dominance. No outside investment. Epic Games — Tim Sweeney started in his parents' basement in 1991. Now valued at $30B+ after Fortnite. Took late strategic investment from Tencent and Sony, but the foundation was bootstrapped for ~20 years. Spanx — Sara Blakely started with $5,000 in savings in 2000. Bootstrapped for 21 years until Blackstone took majority in 2021 at $1.2B valuation. Blakely became a billionaire. Tier 2: Started with personal savings or credit cards (<$50K), eventually took VC after proving the model Atlassian — Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar started 2002 with $10K AUD on credit cards. No VC for 8 years and 40 consecutive profitable quarters. Now ~$40B market cap (NASDAQ: TEAM). Wayfair — Niraj Shah and Steve Conine started with $7K in 2002. Profitable in their first month, no VC until they hit $500M in revenue. Peak $40B, currently ~$6B post-correction. GitHub — Three co-founders bootstrapped from 2008-2012 before raising $100M from a16z. Sold to Microsoft for $7.5B in 2018. GoPro — Nick Woodman started with $10K from selling necklaces with his wife. IPO'd at $11B peak valuation, currently smaller after the action camera market commoditized. Yeti — Roy and Ryan Seiders bootstrapped from making fishing rods. IPO'd at $1.7B in 2018, currently ~$3B. Pluralsight — Aaron Skonnard bootstrapped for years before Insight Partners came in. Sold to Vista Equity for $3.5B in 2021. Calendly — Tope Awotona invested his life savings as part of a $550K seed round, remained capital-efficient for 7 years. Last valued at $3B in 2021. Shutterstock — Jon Oringer started with his own savings and his own photographs. Currently ~$2B market cap. SurveyMonkey — Ryan Finley bootstrapped from 1999, sold to Spectrum Equity in 2009. Was a unicorn at 2018 IPO, currently ~$1B+. Topgolf — Started bootstrapped 2000s, eventually took strategic investment. Now ~$4B+ as part of Topgolf Callaway. ZipRecruiter — Ian Siegel and team bootstrapped as a "lifestyle business" before raising $63M Series A. IPO'd 2021 at ~$2.4B, currently smaller. NerdWallet — Tim Chen bootstrapped 2009-2015 before $64M Series A. IPO'd 2021 around $1.3B. Campaign Monitor — Sydney-based, bootstrapped to scale before a $250M first round from Insight Venture Partners — the first-round size is the tell of how much they'd built on their own. Some legendary "almost bootstrapped" worth knowing: Lululemon — Chip Wilson started with personal savings in 1998. Now ~$35B market cap. Did some early strategic capital but no traditional VC path. Stripe — Often gets called bootstrapped but actually took early YC and angel funding (~$2M seed). Not strictly bootstrapped. WhatsApp — Took some early Sequoia investment but extremely capital-efficient. Sold to Facebook for $19B. Borderline. Patterns worth pulling out, given your serial-entrepreneur context: A few things this list reveals that's relevant for the ParkOS thinking: B2B SaaS dominates the truly bootstrapped tier. Mailchimp, Zoho, Atlassian, Basecamp, Calendly, Pluralsight, Campaign Monitor — recurring revenue businesses with low marginal cost are the most capital-efficient model in history. ParkOS fits this template structurally. The bootstrapped path consistently produces higher founder equity at exit. Wayfair's founders held substantial stakes at $40B peak. Atlassian's founders are still ~30% owners after IPO. Mailchimp's founders split $12B essentially intact. VC dilution typically leaves founders with 10-15% at IPO; bootstrappers often hold 40-70%+. The "no VC for X years" pattern is more common than "never any VC." Most of these companies eventually took some capital — but did so from a position of strength (already profitable, already at scale) which dramatically shifted the terms in founders' favor. The discipline is in when you take capital, not whether you ever do. Vertical-specific software + services (Yeti for outdoor, Spanx for shapewear, Patagonia for outdoor apparel) shows you don't need to be pure tech to bootstrap to billion-dollar scale. Operations-heavy businesses with strong brand equity work too. The clear common thread: all of these companies were profitable early and grew on customer revenue rather than investor capital. The VC playbook of "burn cash to grow then figure out unit economics later" is the opposite of what built every company on this list

Educational Note Of The Day Why "first hour reversals" happen so often after big gap moves When markets gap up significantly at the open (like NQ +1.6% yesterday), the first hour of cash trading frequently sees a reversal or significant pullback. Here's why: 1. Overnight gaps come from futures, not real volume.A gap up of 200+ NQ points is built on relatively thin overnight liquidity. When New York opens at 9:30 AM ET, you suddenly have institutional desks, ETF rebalancing, options market makers, and retail flow ALL hitting the tape at once. The thin gap meets thick volume — and the gap often gets challenged. 2. Gap fade is a real strategy.There are entire institutional desks built around fading opening gaps. The data supports them: roughly 60-65% of gap-ups above 1% see at least a partial fill in the first 60 minutes of cash trading. 3. Overnight news has time to be re-evaluated. At 5 AM CT, you reacted to Trump's tweet emotionally. By 9 AM, smarter desks have read the fine print, considered Iran's official response, checked oil's behavior, and decided whether to chase or fade. That reassessment process IS the morning reversal. The trading framework: Strong gap + strong volume on the open + holds above pre-market high in first 5 minutes = trend day up, lean long Strong gap + weak volume on the open + immediately rejects pre-market high = fade likely, lean short the bounce Strong gap + chop in first 15 minutes = wait, no edge The lesson from yesterday's tape: the bounce held into the close, which means today's gap-up at 9:30 is starting from a stronger foundation than yesterday's was. The legal test for trade dress infringement looks at *likelihood of confusion* among relevant consumers as to source or affiliation—not whether regular Costco members recognize the Kirkland label. Lululemon argues the close similarity in design, cut, and style of the jackets, pants, and hoodies could still lead some shoppers (newer customers, online viewers, or those less brand-savvy) to mistakenly link the cheaper Kirkland versions to Lululemon or assume they're authentic equivalents from the same makers. Costco regulars knowing the difference strengthens Costco's defense, but it doesn't erase the claim if broader evidence of potential confusion exists. Courts weigh multiple factors like product similarity and marketing channels.

That's standard IP enforcement, not frivolous "throwing lawsuits at the wall." Costco can defend on no confusion or functionality grounds. Courts decide based on evidence of distinctiveness and likelihood of confusion.
